### Method Details

#### Protein binding microarray (PBM) experiments

We expressed proteins by either (i) purification from E. coli C41 DE3 cells (Lucigen), or (ii) in vitro translation reactions (Ambion ActivePro Kit and NEB PURExpress) without purification, both as previously described (Badis et al., 2009; Berger et al., 2008). Briefly, GST-TF fusion proteins were either purified from E. coli overexpression cultures by GST affinity chromatography. The quality and concentration of each such GST-tagged protein was estimated relative to a dilution series of GST standards on Coomassie-stained SDS-PAGE gels. Alternatively, GST-TF fusion proteins were expressed by in vitro transcription and translation following the manufacturer’s protocol without subsequent purification. Western blots were performed to assess the quality and to approximate the concentration of each resulting GST-TF fusion protein relative to a dilution series of recombinant GST standards. Custom-designed oligonucleotide arrays (Agilent) were double-stranded and PBM experiments were performed following previously described experimental protocols (Berger et al., 2006). The array designs employed were “all 10mer” universal arrays (Agilent Technologies). Experimental conditions used for all PBM experiments, including gene names, protein expression method, Agilent AMADID numbers, TF concentrations, cloning sequences and TF classes are described in Table S1.

#### PBM data processing

PBM scan images were obtained using a GenePix 4000A Microarray Scanner (Molecular Devices). The resulting image data were processed using GenePix Pro v7.2 to obtain signal intensity data for each spot. The data were then further processed using Masliner software (v1.02) (Dudley et al., 2002) to combine scans from different intensity settings, increasing the effective dynamic range of the signal intensity values. If a dataset had any negative background-subtracted intensity (BSI) values (which can occur if the region surrounding a spot is brighter than the spot itself), all BSI values were scaled such that they all became non-negative. All BSI values were normalized using the software for spatial de-trending provided in the Universal PBM Analysis Suite (Berger and Bulyk, 2009), as previously described (Berger et al., 2006). Briefly, Alexa488 signal was normalized by Cy3 signal for each spot to account for differences in the amounts of double-stranded DNA. To correct for any possible non-uniformities in protein binding, we further adjusted the Cy3-normalized Alexa488 signals according to the position of each spot within a 15 × 15 block centered on each spot on the microarray.

#### PBM evaluation for DNA-binding specificity

We used the Universal PBM Analysis Suite (Berger and Bulyk, 2009) to calculate the PBM enrichment score (E-score) for each of the 32,768 non-redundant, ungapped 8mers for each protein. The E-score is a rank-based statistic that is closely related to the area under the receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve and robust to technical variation across arrays (Berger and Bulyk, 2009). Larger E-score values reflect higher specificity for binding a particular 8mer. The presence of E-scores ≥ 0.45 has been reported as a viable quality control metric to identify successful PBM experiments (Berger et al., 2008; Weirauch et al., 2014). Here, we deemed a PBM experiment to be of acceptable quality if it contained at least five 8mers with an E-score ≥ 0.45.

### Quantification and Statistical Analysis

#### Construction of the glossary

#### Data mining and filtering

We collected 773 good quality PBM arrays (i.e., those that contained at least five 8mers with an E-score ≥ 0.45) representing the sequence specificity of more than 671 metazoan TFs from unpublished experiments, CIS-BP (Weirauch et al., 2014) database, and UniPROBE (Badis et al., 2009) database, noting gene names, organism of origin, original publication and TF classes (Table S1). We combined the E-scores of these PBM arrays into a single data table with each PBM experiment retained in a separate column and each 8mer in a separate row. We used the rank-based PBM enrichment score (E-score) to quantify the preference of a TF for each 8mer (Berger et al., 2006) and used an E > 0.3 threshold to capture preferences for binding to lower affinity sequences (Barrera et al., 2016; Berger et al., 2008). We considered all 8mers with E-score > 0.3 as ‘bound’ by an assayed protein (Barrera et al., 2016), and discarded 8mers that did not exhibit an E-score > 0.45 in at least one experiment. This filter reduced the initial table to the 10,926 8mers (http://thebrain.bwh.harvard.edu/uniprobe/downloads.php).

#### First clustering

We independently clustered the rows and the columns of these data using Pearson correlations as distance and hierarchical agglomerative complete-linkage (“hclust” function in R). From them, we obtained one dendrogram for the 8mers and one for the PBMs (Figure S1a). We created several independent collections of 8mer clusters by repeatedly cutting the 8mer dendrogram with the function “cutreeDynamicTree” (from R package “dynamicTreeCut”, setting: maxTreeHeight=0.9, deepSplit=FALSE). Each dendrogram treecut differed by the minimal cluster size (CMS), which we varied between 20 and 100 8mers (red to orange bars, Figure 1b). To associate specific PBM experiments to each 8mer cluster, we sorted the subtable defined by its 8mers and applied a 2-mean-clustering on the E-score profile to discriminate PBM exhibiting high versus low specificity. The highly specific PBMs then were coupled to the 8mer cluster, to form an 8mer-PBM cluster (black boxes in Figure S1b). We grouped the 8mer-PBM clusters obtained by each individual CMS to form a single CMS collection (i.e., “20 CMS collection”). We evaluated the different cluster collections by the Davies-Bouldin index (DBI) (Davies and Bouldin, 1979), which compares the inter-cluster E-score difference against the intra-cluster E-score similarity (small DBI for good tree cuts). Since cluster collections with smaller DBI tended to filter out more 8mers, we corrected the DBI by the 8mer coverage (Figure S1c).

#### Merged cluster collection

To create a collection of 8mer-PBM merged clusters from the previous single CMS collections, we matched them through a cumulative pairwise comparison (blue to cyan bars, Figure 1b). For the comparison scheme, we started comparing the 20 and 25 CMS collections, creating a “20–25” intermediate collection. The intermediate “20–25” was then compared with the 30 CMS collection to create the “20–30” intermediate collection. This comparison scheme was iterated up to the 100 CMS collection, creating the “20–100” intermediate collection which, after a further comparison with an asymptotic collection formed by a single cluster for the whole 8mer dendrogram, furnished the final Merged Clusters. For the rules of cluster merging between two collections (A and B), we used the following assumption:

- 1-to-1 match: if the 8mers of a cluster from A overlapped uniquely with the 8mers of one and only one cluster from B, we merged their 8mers into a single cluster in the next intermediate collection.

- Cluster rescue: if all the 8mers of a cluster from A did not fall in any cluster of B, we inserted the cluster in the next intermediate collection.

- Neighbor clusters comparison: if the 8mers of two (or more) clusters from collection A jointly overlapped the 8mers of one (or more) clusters from collection B, we cut the 8mer interval in all the possible tree cut intervals suggested by the two tree cuts (dotted lines in Figure 1b), which creates a new set of minimal clusters (green bars in Figure 1b). Within this set, we compared each pair of contiguous 8mer-PBM clusters. To merge two clusters (green arrows in Figure 1b) we first required that their difference in the average E-scores was less than 0.12, as a criterion to ensure that the 8mers of the two clusters exhibit a sufficiently similar overall specificity to the associated TF PBMs. Moreover, within each of the two clusters, we quantified the average E-score of the PBMs over the 8mers. If the overall variability of the average E-score of the PBMs in the two clusters (i.e., the sum of the Standard Deviation of the average E-score for PBMs in the two clusters) was also less than 0.12, we merged the two clusters. If this variability was higher than 0.12, we further required that the average E-score values of the PBMs in the two clusters were positively correlated (Spearman rank correlation coefficient rho (R) > 0.1, P <0.05), to merge 8mer clusters with similar E-score profiles for the associated PBMs. We empirically found that these conditions reliably merged two clusters exhibiting the same E-score pattern across PBM experiments. When compared to the collections obtained by single CMS, the merged cluster collection showed the smallest corrected DBI index (best clustering) (Figure S1c), the highest coverage, and its clusters encompassed the widest range of 8mer sizes (data not shown).

#### Re-clustering

To ensure convergence and robustness of the clustering, we re-clustered the merged cluster collection. To filter out noise, we first assigned the E-score basal value (0.3) to any 8mer-PWM pair not contained in the merged clusters (background filtering). For these filtered data, we obtained 8mer and PBM dendrograms, as described for the first clustering (re-clustering). The background E-score values were then re-assigned to each 8mer-PBM pair (background rescue), and the dendrogram were repeatedly cut and compared to create the merged clusters collection. We renamed this collection as “glossary”, and its 8mer-PBM merged cluster as “TF-8mer module”, naming each module according to the class of the TFs assayed by the most specific PBMs. Overall, the glossary contained 671 non-redundant TFs from 715 PBM datasets and 10,428 8mers. Importantly, each 8mer is assigned to just one module, but the same PBM (and therefore its assayed TF) can be associated with several modules (right panel Figure 1c, middle-right panels in Figure S1d).

#### Evaluation of module purity for TF class

To evaluate how strongly each module was associated to a single TF class, we defined a “Purity Index” for the modules as follows. If all the PBMs associated with a certain module assayed TFs from the same class, then that module’s Purity Index was assigned as 100% (i.e., TEA, IRF and FOX modules in Figure S1d). If the module’s PBMs were assaying TFs from several TF classes, each PBM in the module was assigned its average 8mer E-score (i.e., E-scorePBM = <E-scores(8merscluster, PBM)>). Each TF class was then assigned the highest value of its associated PBMs (i.e., E-scoreTFclassA = max(E-scoreTFclassA_PBM1, E-scoreTFclassA_PBM2, ...). We than ranked the E-scores assigned to all the TF classes presented in the module in a decreasing order (i.e., E-scoreFirst_TFclass > E-scoreSecond_TFclass > …> E-scoreLast_TFclass) and defined the Purity Index as following: Module Purity Index = ( E-score First _ TFclass - E-score Second _ TFclass ) / ( E-score First _ TFclass - E-score Last _ TFclass )

#### Derived PWMs from glossary’s 8mer modules

To build a PWM for each module, we ranked 8mers by their average E-score. We oriented the ranked 8mers using the program PAGAN(Loytynoja et al., 2012), aligned them to create a PWM with the program MAFFT(Katoh and Standley, 2013), and visualize the resulting PWM via the R-package seqLogo (Table S2).

#### Motif enrichment analysis in ChIP-seq peaks

To examine ChIP-seq peaks for the enrichment of a TF binding specificity motif, represented either by a PWM, an 8mer module, or a DeepBind motif model, we calculated the area under receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) statistics to evaluate the enrichment(Weirauch et al., 2013) in the 500 ChIP-seq peak sequences with the highest fold-change above the local distribution of reads modeled by a Poisson distribution (Feng et al., 2011). We trimmed the peaks to encompass a maximum of 200 bp by using the position of the peak center (also referred in the text as peak summit) provided by the original datasets. As the background set, we generated an equally sized set of 500 sequences with one of the methods for background construction discussed in the text and below.

To compute a PWM-based AUROC, each sequence in the foreground and background sets was scanned by the PWM (function “PWMmatch” in R package Biostrings) and then assigned a score corresponding to the best PWM match (function “PWMscoreStartingAt” in R package Biostrings). The position of the best PWM match within the sequence was also recorded and used to evaluate the motif distance from the peak summit. The AUROC statistic was obtained by calculating sensitivity and specificity values as the score threshold for predicting a region to be bound was varied between 0 and the max score.

To compute 8mer-based AUROC for a glossary’s module, we first looked for foreground and background sequences that matched the module’s 8mers, scoring each sequence by the highest E-scores of its matching 8mers. This E-score value represented the binding probability of the sequence to be used in the AUROC analysis. As previously described (Barrera et al., 2016), the AUROC statistic was obtained by calculating sensitivity and specificity values as the E-score threshold for predicting a region to be bound was varied between 0.3 and 0.5 (the range of E-scores used in this study). The P-values associated with each AUROC value were calculated by using a Wilcoxon signed-rank test comparing the scores for foreground and background sequences, which we adjusted with a False Discovery Rate test for multiple hypothesis along the 108 motifs of the glossary. The position of the best-matched 8mer was also used to evaluate the Motif-Summit distance.

For each background methods and TF specificity models, we evaluated across all the combinations of one ChIP-seq dataset and one glossary module: (1) the median absolute deviation (MAD) of the AUROC values and (2) the Spearman rank correlation coefficient rho (R) between AUROC values and Motif-Summit distance. We computed the AUROC MAD through the function “mad” in R-package “stats,” which by definition returns the median of the absolute deviations from the median and adjusts it by a constant for consistency with the standard deviation in case of normal distributions: mad ( Xi ) = 1.483 ∗ median ( ∣ Xi - median ( Xi ) ∣ )

For the values in Figure 3c and Figure 4b, the total number of ChIP-seq-module combinations, which are represented as data points in the plots, are: 239 ChIP-seq datasets × 108 TF- 8 mer modules = 25 , 812

For the TF-family subsets in Figure 3d–e and Figure S4, the total number of ChIP-seq-module combinations varied between 108 (MYB) and 3,780 (bHLH).

To compute the AUROC for sequences analyzed using DeepBind models (Alipanahi et al., 2015), each sequence in the foreground and background sets was scanned using the open source C-code “DeepBind.c” provided in the DeepBind webpage (http://tools.genes.toronto.edu/deepbind/). We used the code’s standard mode, which returns the DeepBind score of the best match. We also developed a “position” option in the “DeepBind.c” code that returns the distance between the best match and the peak summit. Similarly to the PWM case, the AUROC statistic was obtained by calculating sensitivity and specificity values as the threshold of the DeepBind score was varied between 0 and the max score.

In the case of Figure S5, since just 13 PBM datasets representing modules were available as DeepBind motif models, the total number of ChIP-seq-module combinations for each was (239*13) = 3,107.

#### Building Background Sets for ChIP-seq peaks

From the “foreground” dataset of genomic regions defined as a BED file, we obtained the actual sequences with the “getfasta” command from BEDTools (Quinlan, 2014) using the unmasked genome as input. Using the BED file and fasta file as required, we created the following background sets:

#### Dinucleotide Shuffle

We obtained the permuted sequences with identical dinucleotide frequencies and length using uShuffle software (Jiang et al., 2008).

#### Flanking Regions

Genomic regions 1000 bp upstream from the ChIP-seq peak were obtained using the “getfasta” command as for the foreground. We decided to use 1000 bases as an intermediate flanking distance among several proposed in similar analysis (Bailey and Machanick, 2012; Orenstein and Shamir, 2014; Siggers et al., 2011a; Wang et al., 2012a), ranging from 300 to 2000 bp. Notably, the ChIP-seq peaks in the foreground datasets have a median size of 305 bp (+/− 110), ensuring that the flanking regions do not overlap with the actual peaks.

#### GC-BiasAway

We downloaded BiasAway (Worsley Hunt et al., 2014) from https://github.com/wassermanlab/BiasAway/ and the human 200 bp background repository from http://cisreg.cmmt.ubc.ca/BiasAway_background/. After learning that the program was not equipped to handle a directory as a background, we randomly sampled 5000 sequences from each repository 1% bin file and put them into a single fasta file to be used as the background pool file. The BiasAway subcommand ‘g’ (%GC distribution-based background chooser) was used for each foreground ChIP set.

#### GC-HOMER

We used HOMER (Heinz et al., 2010) version 4.6 subprogram findMotifsGenome.pl with the arguments hg19, -size 200, -N 500 to coincide with our foreground set; -dumpFasta to obtain the background fasta file; -nomotif and -noknown to avoid any de novo motif searching.

#### GENRE

We used the hg19 uniquely mappable regions (ENCODE, 2012) subtracted by hg19 blacklisted regions (ENCODE, 2012) as the BED file to be tiled for possible background regions (https://personal.broadinstitute.org/anshul/projects/umap/encodeHg19Female/globalmap_k20tok54.tgz; http://hgdownload.cse.ucsc.edu/goldenPath/hg19/encodeDCC/wgEncodeMapability/wgEncodeDacMapabilityConsensusExcludable.bed.gz, respectively). The chosen matched features from the UCSC hg19 genome version (Speir et al., 2016) were: promoters (defined as 2 kilobases upstream of transcription start sites (TSS) according to strandedness for known genes), repeat regions (Repeat Masker files), GC content and CpG dinucleotides (unmasked genome). The overall binning scheme that we chose was: independently binning promoters and repeats with binary ranges, and then nesting quartiles of GC content and subsequently CpG dinucleotides. The all-but-one analysis seen in Figure S3 utilized the same nested quartile scheme, but removing one feature, i.e., for leaving promoters out, we binned repeats in a binary manner, and for each repeat bin (0/not0), quartiles were nested first for GC content and then for CpG dinucleotides.

#### GENRE implementation and benchmarking

#### Database Construction

GENRE is a background generation tool that builds an a priori database of possible background regions that are matched to foreground regions via user-defined features. It has been implemented using Python, SQLite (with a common mathematical and string function library extension from R package RSQLite written by Liam Healy), and BEDTools (Quinlan, 2014). Initially, a BED file is tiled into uniformly sized regions and loaded into a table in the database. That table is then extended to include the real values associated with each feature’s overlap percentage as calculated by BEDTools (genomic features via “intersectBed” with the feature’s BED file; compositional features via “nucBed” with a fasta file). The user can then decide how to bin features, either by ranges (i.e. binary – “0,(0–100]”), equal percent size (e.g., 5% bins), or nested quartiles (e.g., GC quartiles stratified by promoters). Each binning scheme is housed in its own table within the database.

#### Table binning – Nested Quartiles

GENRE, being able to match for multiple features, can present with a scarcity problem; lesser populated multiplexed background bins may not contain enough sequences from which to build a background set. While background scarcity was only a minor issue for this study, it could potentially become a larger problem for smaller genomes with fewer possible background sequences and analyses that require a background multiple times bigger than the foreground. Giving a nested quartiles option addresses this issue by binning the background to match the overall interdependent feature densities of the foreground with quartiles to modulate bin size (Figure 2c–e, Figure S2). The more populated multiplexed bins will be the same in both the foreground and the background, so there should be little issue finding multiple matches to a foreground region within a proportionally larger background bin. This is done by first finding the independently grouped feature combinations, and then for each group, nesting for loops for every subsequent nesting criterion. Within each for loop, the quartiles of the nesting criterion are found, and the where clause of the query is updated to only include background regions that fall into the independent group combination and individual quartile ranges. The last for loop writes the where clause information into a quartile bin table within the database to be used when mapping foreground regions to background bins.

#### Database Querying for Background

To match a foreground set, each region’s percent overlap is found and binned in the same way as the designated background table. That table’s matching multiplexed bin is randomly sampled without replacement per foreground region for the user-requested multiplicity of background sequences. If all foreground regions find a match, the background set is validated, and a background fasta file is made using “fastaFromBed” of the BEDTools suite and a supplied fasta file.

#### Motif enrichment of highly expressed TFs

We wanted to evaluate whether the enrichment of a motif not bound directly by a ChIPed TF was predictive of the high expression of TFs specific for a cell line. For that, we collected RNA-Seq data from ENCODE (Table S5), which profiled the expression of most of the cell lines assayed in our ChIP-seq datasets. In each cell line, we ranked the genes according to their expression level (FPKM), where low rank indicates high expression. If there were replicate RNA-Seq datasets, the average FPKM was computed and used to rank the cell line expression profile.

For the TF motifs, we focused on the 12 TF families with strong DNA binding preferences (POU, GATA, FOX, KLF, CEBP, MAF, IRF, ETS, TEA, AP2, ZIC and E2A) that play a relevant role in transcriptional control and cellular differentiation (“tethering motifs” list). To compare the different settings used in this study for motif enrichment analysis, we considered the AUROC values obtained previously (Figures 3,4). For each setting, we obtained the AUROC values for the 12 tethering motifs across the ChIP-seq data-sets. To include only tethering interactions between the motif and the ChIPed TF, we sorted out AUROC values coming from cases of direct binding (such as GATA motif enrichment in GATA3 peaks in MCF-7 cells). For the other cases of indirect binding, we selected the ChIP-seq motif pair exhibiting a significant AUROC enrichment (P-value <0.05). For each pair, we then asked whether at least one TF associated to the motif (“tethering TF”) was highly expressed in the cell line assayed by ChIP-seq. The TF was marked as highly expressed if its expression rank was greater than a predefined threshold (i.e., top 3000 genes, see below). If this was the case, we recorded the event as positive. For each of the 12 motifs along the whole ChIP-seq dataset, the count of highly expressed tethering TFs was recorded.

A permutation test was performed for 200 randomly reshuffled genomes(Barrera et al., 2016) to determine the null value of highly expressed TFs per motif. The p-value was calculated as the proportion of times the reshuffled genome found more highly expressed genes than the real genome. A robust Z-score of finding highly expressed potential tethering factors was calculated as follows where x is the number of highly expressed genes in a ChIP-seq set A: Z A = x A - median x MAD

#### Expression rank of lineage-specific TFs

We considered well-established lineage-specific TFs for 7 cell types with publicly available transcriptomic profiles (RNA-Seq data from ENCODE, Table S5): Sox2 (Wang et al., 2012b; Zhou et al., 2016) and POU5F1 (Wang et al., 2012b) in hESC cells, IRF4 (Mendez and Mendoza, 2016) and PAX5 (Mendez and Mendoza, 2016) in B cells, MYOD1 (Fong et al., 2015) in skeletal muscle cells, GATA1/2 (Bresnick et al., 2012) in K562, HNF4A (Nagy et al., 1994) and FOX2 (Lee et al., 2005) in HepG2, and GATA3 (Takaku et al., 2015) in Mcf-7. For each cell type, we independently ordered the genome by expression level (FPKM), and we found that the lineage-specific TFs were within the top 3,000 genes in their respective cell types, but were of lower expression ranks (>5,000) in lineages they do not specify.

#### Predicting binding type from motif enrichment

We identified the glossary’s 8mer modules that showed a significant enrichment of their associated TFs’ DNA binding specificities in at least one of the 239 ENCODE TF ChIP-seq datasets used in this study (Table S3). For example, the TEA module was selected since it was enriched in TEAD4 ChIP-seq peaks in HepG2 cells. This sorting ensured that the enrichment of these modules is bona fide due to the direct binding of a TF to its cognate motif. These modules are: KLF, AP2, RFX, GATA, ETS, FOX, IRF, NFkBp65, HNF4, CEBP, bZIP, MAF, TEA, POU, Hbox, E2A, EGR, GR, E2F_zfC2H2, zfC4, TCF7, bHLH, ETSI, FOXM, ETSIII, ZFP691, ESRR, ARID3, zfC2H2_EGR_RHD.

The enrichment of a module to a ChIPed TF dataset through direct binding (i.e., TEA module enrichment in TEAD4 ChIP-seq for K562, HepG2 and ESC cells; green dots in Figure 6a) were further separated out and reported in Table S4; we refer to these modules as “Direct Module A”. The remaining combinations, which evaluate the potential indirect binding of the ChIPed TF (“Tethered TF A”) through a tethering factor (“Tethering TF B”) that is among the TFs that are specific for the interacting module (“Indirect Module B”), were identified as those with AUROC > 0.6 and distance-to-summit < 40 bp as criteria (black dots in Figure 6a). More precisely, we put these limits on the indirect binding to avoid the bulk of non-enrichment unlikely to yield true results, as suggested by Figure 4a. The schematics of these potential indirect binding mechanisms with their naming schemes are shown in Figure 6b. These analyses indicated: 48 indirect binding interactions (which sometimes occurred in multiple cell lines), 16 of which have been well-validated in previous experimental reports; 19 have been proposed in some previous analysis and are supported by our findings; and 13 are to our knowledge newly identified in this study (Table S6). Table S6 also denotes the percentage of the tethered TF A’s best 500 peaks that contain its own direct motif (i.e., at least one 8mer of Direct Module A within the peak), its potential indirect motif (i.e., at least one 8mer of Indirect Module B within the peak), and both motifs together. We performed a Fisher Exact Test with correction for false discovery rate (FDR) (fisher.test and p.adjust functions in R) to test two hypotheses: the first is to determine whether the co-occurrence of the two motifs within the same peaks is significantly enriched (fisher.test argument: alternative = “greater”), and the second is to determine whether the co-occurrence of the two motifs within the same peaks was significantly depleted (fisher.test argument: alternative = “less”). An example 2×2 contingency table is shown below for the bZIP TF BACH1 putatively being tethered by the MAF family TF MAFK in H1-hESC cells (row 2 in Table S6), indicating a significantly enriched (P < 0.05) co-occurrence of the bZIP and MAF motifs (schematic in Figure 6b).

To further investigate the potential interaction between the Tethered TFs A and their Indirect Module(s) B of Table S6, we analyzed the extent to which the set of ChIP-seq peaks of TFs A and B overlap. We considered the top 500 peaks of every Tethered TF A with a potential indirect interaction. We trimmed each peak to 200 bp, as defined above (see “Analysis of motif enrichment and Motif-Summit distance in ChIP-seq peaks”). Of all the analyzed ChIP-seq datasets (Table S3), we then restricted our analysis to those for which a TF specific to Indirect Module B was also profiled by ChIP-seq in the same cell type (candidate Tethering TF). For each candidate Tethering TF, we then trimmed its ChIP-seq peaks to 200 bp and intersected them with the Tethered TF A file (intersectBed of BEDTools) to determine how many of the Tethered TF A peaks overlapped the Tethering TF B peaks. Mutations in the AARS2 gene are linked to infantile cardiomyopathy; however, the underlying molecular mechanism remains unknown. Here we report that PCBP1, a poly(rC) binding protein, interacts with the AARS2 transcript to mediate its alternative splicing. Cardiomyocyte-specific deletion of Pcbp1 in mice impairs normal splicing and causes premature termination of Aars2, leading to defects in heart development and postnatal lethality. Similarly, mice with a deletion in Aars2 that mimics a diseasecausing splicing lesion display heart developmental abnormalities, reminiscent of those in patients with infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Mechanistically, loss of Pcbp1 or Aars2 in the heart reduces oxidative phosphorylation, a hallmark of patients with AARS2 mutations. This reduction in mitochondrial-encoded proteome activates mitonuclear communication and the unfolded protein response pathway, thereby inducing a compensatory nuclear-encoded mitochondrial gene program. Our findings provide insights into the PCBP1−AARS2 regulatory axis in mitochondrial cardiomyopathy.

Congenital heart disease (CHD) remains the most common birth defect and the leading cause of morbidity and mortality in children worldwide. Although the genetics of many simple Mendelian forms of CHD have been identified, the molecular basis for most other types remains unknown. This may be due to disorders caused by multiple genes and/ or posttranscriptional/posttranslational variations. RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) are key posttranscriptional regulators of RNA metabolism, controlling alternative splicing, RNA stability and translation. Although

RBPs have been implicated in heart development and maturation1–3, the roles of many RBPs remain unknown. After posttranscriptional modification, a key step in protein synthesis is the ‘charging’, or aminoacylation, of transfer RNA (tRNA) by tRNA synthetase. This process involves cytosolic and mitochondrial tRNA synthetases in separate cellular compartments, although all tRNA synthetase genes are encoded in the nucleus. The recessively inherited AARS2 (alanyl-tRNA synthetase 2) mutation was first described in patients with infantile cardiomyopathy associated with defects in oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS)5 (COXPD8, Online Mendelian Inheritance in Man (OMIM): 614096). However, the knock-in mice harboring Aars2 editing domain mutations cause early embryonic lethality before heart formation6, making it challenging to study AARS2 in the context of heart development in vivo. PCBP1 belongs to the poly(rC)-binding protein (PCBP) family of RBPs; there is only one member in invertebrates but four in mammals (PCBP1, PCBP2, PCBP3 and PCBP4)7. The PCBP family plays important roles in posttranscriptional RNA processing, alternative splicing and translation regulation by interacting with pyrimidine-rich motifs in targeted RNAs8–10; they also have unconventional functions in transcription9 and iron trafficking through ferritin11–13. Germline deletion of either Pcbp1 or Pcbp2 in mice is embryonically lethal14, suggesting that they are independently essential during development. We previously generated a hypomorphic Pcbp1 mutant mouse line that exhibits abnormalities in skeletal muscle growth due to defects in the proliferation and differentiation of skeletal muscle myoblasts and satellite cells, through modulation of the microRNA processing pathway15. However, the function of PCBP1 in cardiomyocytes, especially during cardiac development, is unexplored. In the present study, we sought to determine the functional and mechanistic roles of PCBP1 and AARS2 during heart development. Using genetic and biochemical approaches, we discovered an essential role for PCBP1 in heart development by regulating the alternative splicing of Aars2, which is required for its proper function. Genetic deletion of either Pcbp1 or Aars2 in cardiomyocytes leads to a non-compaction cardiomyopathy and a significant reduction in the proteins that constitute the OXPHOS complexes, reminiscent of COXPD8 patients with infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Our findings define a previously unrecognized function for PCBP1 in regulating Aars2 alternative splicing in cardiomyocytes during development, offering insights into the RBP-regulated mechanisms underlying CHD.

Genetic deletion of Pcbp1 in cardiomyocytes leads to noncompaction cardiomyopathy and bifurcated apex formation Pcbp1 is highly expressed in the embryonic heart (Extended Data Fig. 2a). Therefore, we generated myocardial-specific deletion of Pcbp1 (Pcbp1-cKOCtnt) by crossing Pcbp1-Flox mice13,15 with Ctnt-Cre21, which depletes Pcbp1 specifically in embryonic heart cardiomyocytes (Extended Data Fig. 2b,c). Pcbp1-cKOCtnt appeared in expected Mendelian ratios at E12.5, E16.5 and postnatal day 1 (P1). However, Pcbp1-cKOCtnt was underrepresented at P28, indicating perinatal lethality (Extended Data Fig. 2d−h). Additionally, we found that more than 50% of Pcbp1-cKOCtnt mice died within 2 days of birth (Fig. 2a). To investigate the morphological consequences of the myocardial deletion of Pcbp1, we examined the heart at E12.5 (Extended Data Fig. 2i,j), E16.5 (Fig.2b,c) and P1 (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). The E16.5 mutant hearts exhibited a clear bifurcated apex and markedly dilated atria (Fig. 2b) and showed a thinner ventricular wall compared to control hearts (Fig. 2c). Additionally, the ventricular compact zone of the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart exhibited a reduced thickness at both E16.5 and P1 (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2r). We also observed an accumulation of blood clots in both ventricles and atria of mutant hearts, indicating impaired cardiac function (Extended Data Fig. 2k,l). To analyze the heart morphology in greater detail at E12.5, we performed high-resolution episcopic microscopy of the whole embryo, followed by three-dimensional reconstruction22 to assess the ventricular morphology (Extended Data Fig. 2m−s). The Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart displayed a shorter stature with a higher width-to-height ratio (Extended Data Fig. 2o−q) and a markedly thinner compact zone in the left and right ventricles (Extended Data Fig. 2r,s). To determine cardiac function, we performed echocardiograms in neonatal mice. We found that Pcbp1-cKOCtnt pups were born with significantly lower % fractional shortening (%FS) as well as an elevated systolic left ventricular internal diameter at systole (LVID;s), with an unchanged left ventricular internal diameter at diastole (LVID;d), an unchanged left ventricular posterior wall thickness at systole (LVPW;s) and an unchanged left ventricular posterior wall thickness at diastole

(LVPW;d), suggesting ventricular dilation with systolic dysfunction without changes in ventricular wall thickness (Extended Data Fig. 2t−v and Supplementary Table 1). The cardiac function continued to decline at P1 (Extended Data Fig. 2w−y and Supplementary Table 2) and at P2 (Supplementary Table 3), with further reduction in systolic function. The progressive decline in neonatal systolic function aligns with the typical outcome of patients with left ventricular non-compaction (LVNC)23. Together, these findings suggest that PCBP1 is crucial for heart development; its deletion causes non-compaction cardiomyopathy and bifurcated apex formation.

Disrupted cardiomyocyte maturation trajectory in Pcbp1 mutant hearts To investigate molecular changes in the absence of Pcbp1, we performed RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) to profile transcriptomic changes in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt E16.5 hearts. We identified 796 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), 488 upregulated and 308 downregulated, from E16.5 Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 2d). Because a delay in cardiomyocyte maturation is a hallmark of LVNC, we sought to assess the maturation state of the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart using an unbiased approach. We leveraged existing bulk RNA-seq datasets of E10.5/E11.5 (early) and E15.5/ E16.5 (late) heart ventricles from ENCODE24 and constructed gene sets that correspond to ‘Early Embryonic Heart Signature’ and ‘Late Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We then ran our Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart transcriptome against these gene sets using gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) and found that Pcbp1 deficiency in the myocardium caused a positive enrichment of the ‘Early Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Fig. 2e) and a negative enrichment of the ‘Late Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Fig. 2f). These data demonstrated a clear transcriptomic shift and dysregulation in the developmental trajectory of ventricular maturation associated with Pcbp1 deficiency. To validate these findings, we performed in situ hybridization to label chamber maturation-related transcripts in E16.5 hearts. We found that the expression of Myl4, Myl7 (Fig. 2g) and Bmp10 (Fig. 2h) mRNAs was restricted to the atrium in the wild-type control E16.5 heart, consistent with previous studies25,26. However, ectopic expression of these mRNAs was found in the myocardium and trabecular zones of Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 2g,h). These results suggest that Pcbp1 deficiency results in ventricular developmental delay. We observed that Notch2, Jag1 and Hey2 were significantly decreased in the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts at E12.5 and E16.5 (Extended Data Fig. 3c,d,f−h), whereas Nppa expression was highly upregulated (Extended Data Fig. 3e,i). PCBP1 regulates alternative splicing events and exon skipping of Aars2 in the heart To investigate whether PCBP1 regulates alternative splicing in cardiomyocytes, we performed alternative splicing analysis and identified 542 alternatively spliced genes from Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts. These alternatively spliced genes can be classified into five major classes of splicing events: alternative 3′ splice site, alternative 5′ splice site, skipped exon, retained intron and mutually exclusive exon (Fig. 2i and Extended Data Fig. 4a). We identified 341 skipped exon events, accounting for 62.92% of the total detected alternatively spliced events in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 2i,j). Additionally, we found 84 retained intron events, which comprise 15.5% of the alternatively spliced events, and the rest of the categories account for less than 8% each (Extended Data Fig. 4b,d−g). Notably, the alternatively spliced events that we identified in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts showed minimal overlap with those found in HepG2 or K562 cells after PCBP1 small interfering RNA (siRNA) treatment, suggesting that alternative splicing is most likely regulated in a cell-type-specific manner (Extended Data Fig. 4c). We next asked whether alterations in the skipped exon pattern in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts are directly associated with PCBP1 binding. We generated an RNA map of PCBP1-bound mRNA transcripts corresponding to the pattern of their alternatively spliced events in control and Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts at E16.5 (Fig. 2k and Extended Data Fig. 4h−l). PCBP1 eCLIP peaks located at the 5′ and 3′ flanking intronic regions of all alternatively spliced cassette exons were enriched only in the skipped exon loci from the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts. (Fig. 2k, top, and Extended Data Fig. 4h). However, a similar enrichment was not observed for the exon inclusion events or any of the less frequently observed alternatively spliced categories (Fig.2k, bottom, and Extended Data Fig. 4i−l). These data suggest that Pcbp1 may regulate exon skipping to stabilize target transcripts in the developing heart. To better understand the molecular mechanism underlying PCBP1-mediated exon skipping and to identify its regulatory targets, we focused on genes that exhibit skipped exon in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts and that show PCBP1 binding at their 5′ or 3′ splice sites; these analyses identified 34 genes with both features (Fig. 2l). We found that Aars2 exon-16 junction usage was dramatically decreased in the absence of Pcbp1

in both E16.5 and E12.5 hearts (Fig. 2m and Extended Data Fig. 5a−h). This alternative splicing regulation by PCBP1 is cell autonomous, as we observed similar exon skipping in HL-1 cells with Pcbp1 knockdown (Extended Data Fig. 5i−k). Consistent with our previous mapping of PCBP1 binding sites near AARS2 exon-16, loss of Pcbp1 resulted in significant skipping of Aars2 exon-16, supporting a direct role for PCBP1 in regulating this splicing event. Skipping Aars2 exon-16 results in a downstream frameshift, producing premature termination signals (Extended Data Fig. 5l), which likely affect transcript stability and protein translation. Consistent with this prediction, the mRNA level of Aars2, measured by detecting the region spanning exon-14 to exon-15, a common region in all transcript variants, was reduced by 46% and 59%, respectively, at E12.5 and E16.5 in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Extended Data Fig. 5m,n). Similarly, the amount of AARS2 protein in the E16.5 Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts was dramatically reduced to only 13.7% of the control level (Fig. 2n−p). These findings indicate a robust regulatory role for PCBP1 in Aars2 exon-16 skipping and in controlling AARS2 protein levels in the developing heart.

Aars2 exon-16 deletion causes ventricular non-compaction and apex malformation To test the effects of Aars2 exon-16 skipping, we generated floxed Aars2 mice via CRISPR−Cas9 to insert LoxP sites around exon-16 and confirmed correct LoxP site insertions (Extended Data Fig. 6a−e). We also recovered mutants with deletions: Aars2-DEL248 (251 bp in exon-16), Aars2-DEL-IF (320 bp near the 3′ end of exon-15 and an extra nucleotide from exon-17) and Aars2-In70 (43 bp in intron between exon-15 and exon-16) (Extended Data Fig. 6f−k). Heterozygous mutants are viable and fertile, but no viable homozygous embryos were seen after E8.75. The similar early lethality in these mutants shows that Aars2 exon-16 is vital for early survival. Homozygous Aars2 exon-16 LoxP (Aars2-Flox) mice were viable and fertile when homozygous and were used to create a cardiomyocyte-specific Aars2 exon-16 deletion by crossing with Ctnt-Cre mice (Aars2-cKOCtnt) (Fig. 3a). We could not recover viable Aars2-cKOCtnt at P1, despite observing the expected Mendelian ratio at E16.5 (Fig. 3b). The Aars2-cKOCtnt heart at E16.5 had a reduced length with an obvious apex malformation (Fig. 3c). We noted hypertrabeculation and severe myocardium thinning in E14.5 (Extended Data Fig. 6l,m) and E16.5 (Fig. 3d) hearts. These findings show that Aars2 is crucial for heart development; its loss in the myocardium causes a ventricular non-compaction phenotype. Similar to our Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart analysis, Aars2 deficiency in myocardium positively enriched the curated ‘Early Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Extended Data Fig. 6n) and negatively enriched the ‘Late Embryonic Heart Signature’ (Extended Data Fig. 6o). PCBP1 and AARS2 regulate integrated stress response and OXPHOS in embryonic hearts We found unfolded protein response (UPR) as the top upregulated pathway in hearts of Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt mice. GSEA showed that both had significantly increased UPR-related gene expression (Fig. 4a,b). The UPR is a highly conserved protein quality control system that is activated when cells have impaired folding of nascent proteins in the endoplasmic reticulum30 or in the mitochondria during mitochondrial dysfunction31. Mitochondrial dysfunction also induces the integrated stress response (ISR), a branch of UPR mediated by ATF4 (refs. 32–39). UPR/ISR targets such as Ddit3, amino acid nutrient stress gene Asns40 as well as Atf4 were also elevated in both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt (Fig. 4c−e,i) and Aars2-cKOCtnt (Fig. 4f−h,k) hearts. Furthermore, the protein level of ATF4 and Ser51 p-eIF2α was about twice as high in both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts at E16.5 (Fig. 4j,l). Because p-eIF2α can be activated by both ISR and UPR, we sought to characterize other UPR arms independent of eIF2α phosphorylation. Upon UPR activation, endoplasmic reticulum-bound ATF6 is cleaved to produce a nuclear form (ATF6-N), which contains the bZIP DNA binding and transactivation domains, and act as a potent transcription factor41,42. We assayed ATF6-N levels by western blotting and found that it was elevated in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt embryonic hearts at E16.5 but not in Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts (Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). We examined endoplasmic

reticulum chaperone GRP78 (BiP), XBP1-s, HSP60 and phosphorylation of IRE1, GCN2 and PERK in E16.5 hearts but found no protein-level differences in either Pcbp1-cKOCtnt or Aars2-cKOCtnt embryonic hearts (Extended Data Fig. 7a−d). However, LONP1, the main protease in the mitochondrial matrix that degrades damaged proteins, was elevated in Aars2-cKOCtnt but not in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). The differences in the UPR/ISR response between Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt embryonic hearts, particularly in ATF6 and LONP1, may explain the difference in severity of their phenotypes. Our data show that the eIF2α-ATF4 arm of the UPR/ISR is consistently activated when either Pcbp1 or Aars2 is deleted in the myocardium. We also saw an overall increase in aminoacyl-tRNA transferase (ARS) in both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts (Extended Data Fig. 7e,f), with 11 cytosolic ARS transcripts upregulated in both models (Extended Data Fig. 7g). Cytosolic ARS activation, linked to stress response, was previously associated with transcriptional activation via ATF4 (ref. 43). These findings indicate that loss of Pcbp1−Aars2 results in a unified shift in the UPR/ISR stress response in both models. AARS2 mutation in congenital cardiomyopathy causes OXPHOS deficiency, showing reduced complex I (C-I) proteins and variable reduction in other complexes5,17. Intriguingly, we found that the nuclear-encoded OXPHOS-related genes are significantly downregulated in the hearts of both Pcbp1-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOCtnt mice (Fig. 5a,b). UQCRC2 (C-III) and vATP5A (C-V) levels were notably decreased in Aars2-cKOCtnt hearts but not in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt hearts (Fig. 5c,e). Myh6-Cre44, a cardiomyocyte-specific Cre driver with late-gestation onset, to generate Myh6-Cre;Aars2-Flox/Flox mice, referred to as Aars2-cKOMyh6. Aars2-cKOMyh6 mice exhibit early lethality; all died by P66 with a median survival of 50 days (Fig. 6a). Although heterozygous (Aars2-cHetMyh6) mice show normal cardiac morphology, Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts enlarge progressively, visible at P42 and P56, with increased ventricular weight (Fig. 6b,c and Extended Data Fig. 8a−f). Echocardiography revealed normal function at P7 and P14, but, by P21, LVID;d and LVID;s increased, indicating chamber dilation without functional impact. By P28, %FS declined with further dilation and wall changes, suggesting reduced systolic function. Dilation worsened by P42, with %FS dropping to 7.10 ± 3.80 compared to controls (approximately 42.9), indicating severe heart failure (Fig. 6d,e and Supplementary Tables 4−8). Consistent with these findings, we observed severe cardiac dilation and ventricular wall thinning via hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining (Fig. 6f, top), along with cardiac fibrosis detected by Sirius Red/Fast Green staining at P56 (Fig. 6f, bottom). Transmission electron microscopy at P21 shows a decrease in mitochondrial cristae density in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, whereas sarcomere structure remains normal in both Aars2-cKOMyh6 and control animals (Fig. 6g, top, and Fig. 6h). By P42, sarcomere disarray becomes evident, with M-bands absent; mitochondria display defective structures with fewer cristae and smaller size in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts (Fig. 6g, bottom, and Fig. 6i and Extended Data Fig. 8g). These observations demonstrate that Aars2-cKOMyh6 animals develop a progressive dilated cardiomyopathy, marked by diminished cardiac contractility and severe heart failure in later stages, likely contributing to the postnatal lethality. The reduced cristae at P21, before cardiac decline, suggests that mitochondrial dysfunction is likely the primary cause of cardiac dysfunction. Examining electron transport chain (ETC) protein complexes via native electrophoresis with mitochondrial proteins from Aars2-cKOMyh6 and control hearts revealed reduced C-I, C-III and C-IV supercomplexes in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts at P21, P42 and P56 (Fig. 6j and Extended Data Fig. 8h,k). In-gel activity (IGA) assays showed a severe decrease in enzymatically active supercomplexes in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts across all ages (Fig. 6k,l and Extended Data Fig. 8i−s). This is consistent with our observation

under denaturing conditions, where the catalytic core and protein components of C-I, C-III and C-IV were compromised at the protein level, as shown in both whole-heart lysates and isolated mitochondria (Fig. 6m and Extended Data Fig. 8t−w). Interestingly, no reduction in protein level was detected for the components of C-II (SDHB) and C-V (vATP5A). The impact of Aars2 deficiency on the activity and protein levels of the C-I, C-III and C-IV complexes was consistent with recent studies using patient samples5,45. Additionally, we observed a consistent reduction in the catalytic core components of C-I and C-IV across the respirasomes and supercomplexes containing C-I and C-IV, whereas C-II supercomplexes remained unaffected (Extended Data Fig. 8x,y). Overall, our Aars2-cKOMyh6 model recapitulated key features of congenital mitochondrial cardiomyopathy and suggests that the loss of ETC components from C-I and C-IV precedes the onset of cardiac dysfunction and sarcomere disarray.

Late-onset myocardial Aars2 deficiency leads to an activation of UPR/ISR In line with our embryonic heart findings, we postulate that Aars2 deficiency-driven mitochondrial dysfunction in Aars2-cKOMyh6 mice will cause similar UPR/ISR in the heart. To test this, we examined P21 and P42 samples for the expression of key components of UPR/ISR. We observed activation of PERK and GCN2 via phosphorylation at P21 (Extended Data Fig. 9a). These two proteins are key sensors of the ISR, with PERK also involved in the UPR33. In the mutant hearts at P21, levels of p-eIF2α, ATF4 and ASNS were increased, and they rose further at P42, along with the upregulation of LONP1, a downstream target of ATF4 (Fig. 6n and Extended Data Fig. 9b). Moreover, UPR target genes endoplasmic reticulum chaperone GRP78 (BiP), phosphatase GADD34, ATF6-N and CHOP were elevated in the Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts at P21 (Extended Data Fig. 9c,d). Our data show that loss of Aars2 activates both UPR and ISR responses, with sustained eIF2α phosphorylation. A human COXPD8 sample with AARS2 mutations45 also showed increased eIF2α phosphorylation, ASNS and LONP1 (Extended Data Fig. 9e,f). Additionally, AARS2 protein levels in the human COXPD8 patient’s heart were lower than in normal samples (Extended Data Fig. 9d), aligning with previous findings that mutations in the AARS2 editing domain cause protein instability17. Overall, AARS2 deficiency triggers UPR/ISR activation in the heart.

Loss of Aars2 in the heart results in the activation of the nuclear-encoded mitochondrial translation program and mitonuclear communication To understand the molecular mechanisms of mitochondrial cardiomyopathy caused by Aars2 deficiency, we performed RNA-seq and tandem mass tag (TMT) proteomics on P14 and P21 Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts (Fig. 7a and Extended Data Fig. 10a,b). We integrated transcriptomic and proteomic results at both timepoints. At P14, 234 genes changed only in transcript levels, 314 only in protein levels and 33 in both (Extended Data Fig. 10c). At P21, more genes showed differences, especially in transcriptome analysis: 1,402 in transcript levels, 525 in protein levels and 333 in both (Fig. 7a). Most genes regulated by both RNA and protein at either timepoint were concordant with linear RNA−protein relationships (Fig. 7b and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Aars2, from which exon-16 was conditionally deleted, was significantly reduced at RNA and protein levels at both times (Fig. 7b and Extended Data Fig. 10d). Mitochondrial-encoded proteins were substantially reduced in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, consistent with the role of Aars2 in mitochondrial translation (Fig. 7c). Protein-only downregulated genes were overrepresented in mitochondrial respiratory chain/OXPHOS pathways, indicating an overall translational defect of OXPHOS complexes (Extended Data Fig. 10e,f). Because mitochondrial translation must be coordinated for proper assembly of the OXPHOS system46, the overall reduction in mitochondrial-encoded proteins observed in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts aligns with the OXPHOS defects seen in both Aars2-cKOCtnt and Pcbp1-cKOCtnt embryos. Conversely, genes that are upregulated in both RNA and protein levels in P21 Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, such as MTHFD2, PHGDH, ASNS, SLC7A5, PYCRL, PSAT1 and LONP1, are known to be activated by the mitochondrial UPR/ISR pathway. This supports our conclusion that PCBP1 and AARS2 are key regulators of the stress response. Additionally, in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts, five mitochondrial-encoded proteins (MT-ND2, MT-ND5, MT-CO1, MT-CO2 and MT-CO3) are discordantly regulated, with increased transcripts but decreased protein levels (Fig. 7b). These results suggest that mitochondrial translation defects may trigger a compensatory response, leading to transcriptional activation of these genes. To test if Aars2 loss triggers mitochondrial−nuclear communication in the heart, we performed hierarchical clustering of 376

nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins regulated in Aars2-cKOMyh6 and control hearts at two timepoints (Fig. 7d). We found four regulation patterns forming distinct clusters (clusters I−IV), with proteins in clusters I and II being significantly upregulated and those in clusters III and IV downregulated (Fig. 7d). Pathway enrichment analysis using Gene Ontology terms ‘Molecular Function’ and ‘Biological Process’ revealed different pathways in each cluster, matching their regulation direction. Downregulated proteins (clusters III and IV) were overrepresented in OXPHOS pathways, whereas upregulated ones (clusters I and II) were overrepresented in mitochondrial translation pathways (Fig. 7e and Extended Data Fig. 10g). Because mitochondrial translation defects occur before the induction of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial proteins, this suggests a likely sequence of events: (1) an initial downregulation of mitochondrial-encoded genes, followed by (2) an upregulation of nuclear-encoded mitochondrial translation genes, possibly as a compensatory response to worsening mitochondrial translation defects.

Mechanism for activation of mitonuclear communication by loss of Aars2 To identify the activated transcription program in response to defective mitochondria as a consequence of mitochondrial-nuclear communication, we performed upstream transcription factor predictions for proteins in clusters I and II. Among nine predicted upstream transcription factors, ‘MYC ENCODE’ was the most prominent candidate (Fig. 7f), with only Myc expression upregulated in both P14 and P21 Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts at the mRNA level (Fig. 7g,h). Additionally, MYC protein levels are elevated in Aars2-cKOMyh6 hearts at P42. We reanalyzed published RNA-seq and Myc chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP−seq) datasets from MYC-activated murine hearts, where acute MYC activation was induced by tamoxifen on a MycERT2 transgene47. By intersecting genes significantly upregulated 4 hours after MycERT2 activation with MYC ChIP−seq peaks near promoters, we identified MYC-dependent transcriptional targets. This yielded 425 genes that were both upregulated in MycERT2 hearts and contained MYC ChIP−seq binding sites, termed the ‘Myc Activation Signature in Heart’ (Fig. 7j). Ribosomal biogenesis primarily occurs at the nucleolus, and its activation leads to enlargement of the nucleolar structure50. Notably, MYC activity has been implicated in regulating nucleolar and ribosome biogenesis51,52. We observed a striking nucleolar enlargement in cardiomyocytes deficient in Aars2 (Fig. 7m,n), supporting that activated Myc transcription increased ribosomal biogenesis in the heart. Discussion Mutations of the Aars2 gene, including those that affect its splicing, are linked to human congenital mitochondrial cardiomyopathy5,53. In the present study, we generated mouse models to demonstrate that cardiomyocyte-specific Aars2 mutations cause cardiac defects in embryonic and postnatal hearts, mimicking those observed in patients. Our studies implicate PCBP1, an RBP that directly interacts with Aars2 RNA to regulate its splicing, as a crucial molecule required for proper AARS2 function; furthermore, genetic deletion of Pcbp1 in cardiomyocytes phenocopies cardiac defects found in Aars2 mutant mice. We found that loss of PCBP1−AARS2 in cardiomyocytes reduces mitochondrial and OXPHOS function. Pcbp1 and Aars2 mutant mice also exhibit an activation of the UPR/ISR pathway and enhanced mitonuclear communication. Our study highlights an important role for PCBP1 in cardiac development and function by regulating Aars2 exon-16 inclusion, providing a molecular explanation for how Aars2 mutations cause infantile mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (Fig. 8). Mechanistically, we found that PCBP1 plays a pivotal role in regulating Aars2 alternative splicing and gene expression in cardiomyocytes during heart development. We and others previously found that germline knockout of Pcbp1 causes preimplantation lethality before heart formation, indicating its role during gastrulation14,15. A nonsense variant of human PCBP1, c.550 C > T, is likely pathogenic, with clinical features including developmental delay, short stature, Tetralogy of Fallot and decreased muscle mass54. These support a

role for PCBP1 in heart development and link mutations to congenital heart defects. Cardiomyocyte-specific knockout of Pcbp1 resulted in perinatal lethality, non-compaction cardiomyopathy and defects in ventricular apex formation, underscoring the essential role of Pcbp1 in cardiac development. Our study reveals the role of PCBP1 in RNA splicing, specifically its regulation of Aars2 alternative splicing in the Pcbp1-cKOCtnt heart, in which exon-16 is skipped. Our eCLIP−seq, RIP and minigene experiments support the conclusion that PCBP1 stabilizes this splicing by binding to mRNA. Loss of Pcbp1 causes Aars2 exon-16 skipping, and mutation of PCBP1 motifs flanking Aars2 exon-16 also leads to skipping. Therefore, PCBP1 likely acts as a splicing modulator55, with future work aimed at identifying other ribonucleoprotein complexes involved. AARS2-related infantile cardiomyopathy involves a recurrent pathogenic p.Arg592Trp mutation in the editing domain, found in homozygous or compound heterozygous patients17. Data from modeling the human AARS2 p.Arg592Trp and p.Arg580Trp mutations suggest that these mutations cause a reduction of AARS2 protein and are sufficient to cause a severe defect in mitochondrial protein synthesis. Additional AARS2 damaging mutations have recently been reported in the intronic splice donor site (c.2255+1 G > A) and acceptor site (c.2146-2 A > G) flanking exon-16 of the AARS2 gene56,57, and our experimental data suggest that such mutations cause AARS2 mRNA mis-splicing and loss of function. We speculate that our loss-of-function Aars2 mouse models, which also display mitochondrial translation defects, share a similar pathological mechanism with the human disease. Our Aars2-cKOCtnt mice are embryonically lethal and exhibit LVNC, as do Pcbp1-cKOCtnt mice. Both display OXPHOS deficiency, indicating that they are in the same regulatory axis, linking AARS2-related infantile cardiomyopathy to exon-16 splicing in patients. Aars2-cKOCtnt has a more severe phenotype, likely due to earlier Aars2 deficiency (Cre recombination), compared to Pcbp1-cKOCtnt, where Pcbp1 deletion and Aars2 mis-splicing take longer and require more steps. Furthermore, there may be additional PCBP1-dependent, AARS2-independent pathways that oppose the damaging effects from Aars2 depletion. axis and test if Aars2 overexpression rescues cardiac defects in Pcbp1-cKOCtnt mice. From late gestation, more than half of the ATP generated in the heart relies on OXPHOS, and this balance shifts toward further reliance on OXPHOS after birth58, which is essential for postnatal cardiomyocyte development and maturation59. Direct perturbation of OXPHOS in the embryonic heart can lead to severe heart defects and lethality60–62. The results of our genetic approach to delete the Aars2 gene in embryonic and postnatal mouse hearts confirm its function in heart development and cardiomyopathy. We also found that destabilization of C-I and C-IV occurred in Aars2-cKOMyh6 mice before the onset of cardiomyopathy, indicating that the assembly and turnover of C-I and C-IV are more sensitive to mitochondrial translational defects caused by Aars2 deficiency and are likely the primary causes of the mitochondrial catastrophe that follows. Our finding is consistent with the notion that the turnover of unassembled OXPHOS subunits occurs primarily at the protein level via mitochondrial proteases63,64, and the precise mechanism underlying the selective sensitivity warrants further exploration. We identified MYC as a key transcription factor activated by Aars2 loss of function, promoting mitochondrial and ribosomal biogenesis. Because AARS2 regulates mitochondrial translation, the observed defects and nuclear activation of the UPR/ISR and MYC programs are likely linked as part of retrograde mitonuclear communication in response to cellular stress. Interestingly, MYC can upregulate ATF4 by activating GCN2 via uncharged tRNAs, and ATF4 and MYC co-occupy the promoter of some MYC targets, regulating amino acid and protein synthesis65. It remains to be seen if this transcriptional crosstalk occurred similarly in mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. Our data show that the PCBP1−AARS2 axis induces UPR/ISR, possibly by disrupting mitotranslation, and activates MYC and ATF4. Further studies are needed to identify the downstream targets and pathways regulated by this axis in cardiac development and CHD. Our findings reveal how the RBP PCBP1 regulates splicing of the mitochondrial tRNA aminoacyl transferase AARS2, which is linked to mitochondrial cardiomyopathy. The PCBP1−AARS2 axis safeguards mitochondrial translation and stabilizes OXPHOS complexes in the heart. Given the lack of effective treatments for OXPHOS deficiency diseases, our study advances understanding of the tissue-specific regulatory mechanisms involved and may identify potential therapeutic targets.

Methods All murine experiments were performed in accordance with approved protocols of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Boston Children’s Hospital and the University of Southern California. All research involving human subjects was conducted in accordance with approved protocols of the University of Rochester Institutional Review Board.

Animal husbandry and gene manipulations CRISPR−Cas9 pronuclear microinjection was used to generate Aars2-Flox and deletion mutant mice at the Mouse Gene Manipulation Core of Boston Children’s Hospital as previously described66 with minor modifications. In brief, a cocktail of 0.61 pmol µl−1 each of crRNA+tracrRNA, 100 ng µl−1 Cas9 protein and 10 ng µl−1 ssODN (Integrated DNA Technologies (IDT)) or ds-Donor DNA was injected into the pronuclei of E0.5 embryos (C57BL6/Harlan). Surviving embryos were reimplanted into recipient CD1 pseudo-pregnant females and allowed to develop to term. The resultant pups were genotyped by polymerase chain reaction (PCR), and genome-edited founders were identified and verified by TOPO cloning followed by Sanger sequencing. Two founders were chosen from each line and backcrossed to C57BL/6 (Harlan) for three generations to establish lines. Genotyping primers for screening founders are listed in Supplementary Table 9.

We obtained a Pcbp1-Flox allele13 for conditional knockout generation. Mice carrying Pcbp1-Flox or Aars2-Flox were bred with Tg(Tnnt2-cre)5Blh/JiaoJ (Ctnt-Cre)21 or Tg(Myh6-cre)2182Mds/J44 to generate corresponding cardiac-specific conditional deletions (Pcbp1-cKOCtnt, Aars2-cKOCtnt and Aars2-cKOMyh6). All data presented here for Pcbp1-cKOCtnt are from the previously described nonhypomorphic Pcbp1-Flox allele13, although we also examined our independently generated hypomorphic Pcbp1-Flox allele15 for conditional knockout and observed a very similar phenotype. All animals were maintained on a 12-hour light cycle, at specific pathogen-free facilities. Genetically modified strains of mice were genotyped by isolating genomic DNA from a tail tip excision and subjecting the DNA to PCR using primers corresponding to the modification. For timed pregnancy experiments, 2-month-old males and females from indicated lines and genotypes were co-housed, and the vaginal plugs of the female mice were checked each morning after the date of co-housing to approximate the date of gestation, with the day of vaginal plug appearance noted as E0.5. Mice were euthanized by CO2 asphyxiation according to approved protocols.

Human tissue Heart tissue from a single COXPD8 patient (diagnosed premortem) and three unrelated comparison patients, who died from various causes between 1 day and 5 months of life, were authorized for research and provided, with deidentified clinical data, through the Developmental Lung Molecular Atlas Program (LungMAP) Human Tissue Core and BioRepository for Investigation of Neonatal Disease of the Lung (https://brindl.urmc.rochester.edu/labkey/home/project-begin.view), managed by Gloria Pryhuber (University of Rochester). Deidentified clinical metadata and next-of-kin authorizations for each heart sample used in research were provided by the Organ Procurement Organizations. Aliquots of heart samples were harvested and frozen at −80 °C for experimental use. Details are presented in Beutner et al45.

Differentiation of hiPSC-CMs hiPSC-CMs were generated using the STEMdiff Ventricular Cardiomyocyte Differentiation Kit (STEMCELL Technologies, 05010) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. In brief, a mono-allelic mEGFP-tagged ACTN2 WTC iPSC line (ACTN2−EGFP; AICS-0075-085 from the Coriell Institute for Medical Research) was seeded at 80,000 cells per well in mTeSR1 Plus with 10 µM Y-27632 in 12-well plate wells precoated with hESC-qualified Matrigel matrix (Corning, 354277) according to the manufacturer’s protocols. The next day, media were refreshed without Y-27632. When cell coverage reached 50% confluency, usually 2−3 days after seeding, day 0 medium was added. Media conditions were changed exactly every 48 hours; by days 7−10, cells were observed to be beating. Between days 11 and 14 of differentiation, cells were dissociated using Accutase (Corning, 25-058-CI). ACTN2−EGFP cells were incubated with DRAQ7 membrane-impermeable dye (1:100) and sorted on DRAQ7−ACTN2−EGFP+ single cells. For splicing minigene experiments with a fluorescence reporter, we use the WTC-Cas9 line derived from WTC-11 (ref. 67) to avoid conflicts with the green fluorescence channel. WTC-Cas9 cells underwent the same differentiation procedure as described above. For hiPSC-CM purification, we used the Miltenyi iPSC-CM Isolation Kit (Miltenyi Biotec, 130-110-188) following the manufacturer’s protocol. Purified or sorted hiPSC-CMs were seeded in passaging medium for 48 hours and then changed to expansion medium (STEMCELL Technologies, 100-1109). Cells were maintained in expansion medium with every other day feeding until used for downstream experiments.

High-resolution episcopic microscopy and three-dimensional reconstruction Mouse embryos were processed for high-resolution episcopic microscopy as described previously22. In brief, E12.5 embryos were fixed in 10% neutral buffered formalin solution at 4 °C for 72 hours. Embryos were then incubated in clearing solution (4 M urea, 10% glycerol and 4% sodium dodecyl sulfate in double distilled water) for 8 days at room temperature, and the solution was replaced every 2 days. Cleared embryos were subsequently washed in PBS three times for 5 minutes each and dehydrated in ascending ethanol series (50%, 60%, 70%, 80%, 85%, 90%, 95% and 100% ethanol) at room temperature with gentle rocking for 2 hours at each step. The dehydrated embryos were stained with staining solution (0.1375 g of Eosin Y Disodium and 0.0275 g of Acridine Orange hemi(zinc chloride) salt in 50 ml of ethanol) for 1 hour and then replaced with fresh staining solution to stain overnight. Infiltration solution (100 ml of Solution A of JB-4 embedding kit, 1.25 g of Catalyst C, 0.275 g of Eosin Y Disodium Salt and 0.055 g of Acridine Orange hemi(zinc chloride) salt) was made, and the stained embryos were first incubated in a 1:1 mixture of staining solution and infiltration solution for 3 hours in 4 °C, then in 100% infiltration solution for 3 hours in 4 °C and then in fresh infiltration solution for 72 hours in

4 °C. The solution was changed every 24 hours. The processed embryos were then embedded in resin material as described previously22, and the embedded blocks were mounted on a microtome. The cut face was aligned with a stereo zoom microscope horizontally with the camera acquisition based on excitation 470 ± 20 nm, dichroic 495 nm and emission 525 ± 25 nm. Each section was cut at 2.5 μm, and, with each cut, an image was acquired until the entire embryo was completed. Three-dimensional reconstruction, visualization and measurements were performed using Amira software (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 2019.1).

Histology Mouse heart tissues were dissected out, rinsed with PBS and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde (pH 7.4) overnight. After dehydration through a series of ethanol baths, samples were embedded in paraffin wax according to standard laboratory procedures. Sections of 5 μm were stained with H&E. The stained sections were used for routine histological examination by light microscopy and quantified with ImageJ software (National Institutes of Health).

Echocardiography Echocardiographic measurements were performed on neonatal mice using a Vevo 2100 Imaging System (Visual Sonics) with a 40-MHz Micro- Scan transducer (model MS-550D). Heart rate and left ventricular dimensions, including diastolic and systolic wall thicknesses and left ventricular end-diastolic and end-systolic chamber dimensions, were measured from two-dimensional short-axis under M-mode tracings at the level of the papillary muscle. Left ventricular mass and functional parameters, such as %FS and % ejection fraction (%EF), were calculated from the primary measurements using the accompanying software (Vevo Lab; Visual Sonics).

Immunofluorescence labeling Mouse embryos and embryonic hearts were harvested at different stages and fixed in ice-cold PBS containing 4% paraformaldehyde overnight at 4 °C. Fixed embryos were washed with PBS and then saturated in a 30% sucrose solution in PBS for 6 hours in 4 °C, followed by a 30-minute incubation with 1:1 Optimal Cutting Temperature (O.C.T.) compound (Tissue-Tek):30% sucrose and embedded in O.C.T. compound. Frozen blocks were then cut into 8-μm sections using a Leica CM 3050S cryostat (Leica Microsystems). For paraffin-embedded tissue sections, they were first deparaffined and rehydrated using xylene followed by washes in descending ethanol series (100%, 95%, 70% and 50%) and water. Deparaffined slides were then processed for antigen retrieval using Retrievagen A (pH 6.0) (BD Biosciences) according to the manufacturer’s protocol. Antigen-retrieved slides were then processed for immunofluorescence staining as below. Sections were permeabilized with wash buffer (PBS with 0.2% Triton X-100) and then blocked with blocking buffer (PBS with 1% BSA, 5% donkey serum and 0.2% Triton X-100) for 1 hour at room temperature, followed by overnight incubation at 4 °C with primary antibody diluted in blocking buffer. Sections were rinsed in wash buffer and incubated with fluorescently conjugated secondary antibodies and DAPI diluted in blocking buffer at room temperature for 1 hour, before rinsing and mounting in ProLong Glass mounting medium (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Sections were imaged using an Olympus FluoView FV3000 confocal microscope (n = 4 hearts per group), and at least four sections of the heart were imaged and examined. Detailed antibody information is provided in Supplementary Table 10.
